title_original: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall Review: Paul Thomas Anderson’s Otherworldly Ode to Musical Genius
excerpt_original: On December 11, 2025, Geese frontman Cameron Winter played to a sold-out audience at Carnegie Hall. For the near-entirety of his 12-song performance, he’s hunched over a piano, bathed in a warm overhead light, his shadow cast across the stage. The audience sits much differently…

blocks.text: On December 11, 2025, Geese frontman Cameron Winter played to a sold-out audience at Carnegie Hall. For the near-entirety of his 12-song performance, he’s hunched over a piano, bathed in a warm overhead light, his shadow cast across the stage. The audience sits much differently than they might at a Geese concert: with quiet, rapt patience rather than rowdy screaming and pushing. While in the midst of One Battle After Another ‘s roll-out and awards campaign, Paul Thomas Anderson captured the intimacy of this performance for Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall , and the result is an astonishing 75-minute immortalization of its subject’s genius.

Anderson and producer Benny Safdie handle camera duties as Carnegie Hall’s security opens and closes doors for the filmmakers to walk throughout the stage, swirling around Winter as he methodically goes through released and unreleased songs. He speaks little to the audience, focused only on the piano in front of him. Anderson seems unable to resist Cameron and this opportunity for a level of intimate closeness not even those in the hall’s audience can experience. He rests a camera inches from Winter’s face, blocking out any semblance of the Carnegie crowd, hoping viewers bask in this young rocker’s stardom and accompanying melodies. Anderson sees the then-23-year-old as otherworldly; he wants us to see that, too. The light makes him look almost angelic, ethereal, heavenly, even if his songs and lyrics might not match that image.

For Winter, the sparse, piano-only performance is a showcase. He begins with the unreleased “It All Fell in the River,” and Winter’s voice begins clear and strong. Anderson uses the scale of Carnegie Hall to his advantage, flashing the majesty and familiarity of the theater. He tries to make Winter seem small in comparison to the piano, even smaller in comparison to the venue.

But Winter undeniably has a stage presence despite his lack of movement or conversation. He holds your attention as he taps on a single key. When he gets up from his seat just once before leaving the stage, it’s for a physical-comedy bit seen in wide shot as the audience chuckles at this odd, brief intermission. Then he sits back down and goes into his next song, taking only seconds between each ballad. Winter simply pushes his shaggy hair out of the way, adjusts his sheen-black outfit, and begins again.

If Winter’s (or his band’s) music is new to you, this is likely the most palatable version of such: a stripped-down showcase showing his distinct voice and skill. Anderson understands the juxtaposition of Winter, this early-20s (sometimes punk) rocker, surrounded by the splendor, spectacle, and gentility of midtown Manhattan. All of that—including Anderson’s decision to often hold steady during single takes as Winter sings through large portions of his solo discography—doesn’t matter if the music itself isn’t strong. Luckily, Winter’s songs are filled with complexity and oddity, satisfying melodies paired with unique vocal range.
After only a few songs, it becomes easy to understand why Winter’s not speaking more to the audience. His talent is more than enough of a statement.
Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall begins a theatrical tour on Friday, November 20.
